title: Heidegger and Merleau-Ponty
summary: Phenomenology is a philosophy that tries to describe experience as it is lived from the inside, rather than explain it “from the outside.” Heidegger explored how a person always already lives in the world, cares about it and is attuned to it; Merleau-Ponty showed that this experience is bodily from the very start: we don't “have” a body, we are the body through which we have a world.
onEmotions: For Heidegger, feelings are not “inner states” locked up in the head but “attunement” (Befindlichkeit): the way the world is always already disclosed to us, before any reflection. We are never “out of mood” — even flat indifference is a mood. So a feeling doesn't distort reality; it shows us something about it. Merleau-Ponty adds that feeling lives in the body — in breath, posture, gesture — and that this is not an obstacle to understanding but its first, bodily form.

anxiety.text: Anxiety is not a malfunction or a sign of weakness. Heidegger distinguished fear from anxiety (Angst): fear is always directed at something definite, while anxiety is directed at nothing in particular. In it, the familiar world seems to lose its weight, and a person is left alone with the fact that their life is theirs alone and no one else will live it for them. Heidegger called such states “attunement” (Befindlichkeit) — the way the world is always already disclosed to us. A mood doesn't get in the way of seeing; it is itself a way of seeing. So anxiety can be not only muffled but also listened to: often it tells you that other people's “generally accepted” answers no longer fit you. Merleau-Ponty would add that anxiety lives in the body — in your breath, in your shoulders — and that this too is a way of being in the world, not a mistake.
anxiety.practice: Instead of “How do I get rid of this?” ask yourself: “What has stopped being self-evident for me right now?” Write down one answer.

fear.text: Fear is a legitimate reaction of a living being, and there's no reason to be ashamed of it. For Heidegger, fear is one kind of attunement: it is always fear “in the face of” something approaching and threatening, and fear “about” something — most often about yourself or what is dear to you. That is its honesty: you can only be afraid for what matters to you. Heidegger called this basic feature of human beings “care” (Sorge): something always matters to us; we can't be truly indifferent to our own lives. Merleau-Ponty would remind us that fear is bodily first: the body “knows” about danger before thought does, and it tenses to protect you. To accept fear is to see in it not cowardice but a form of care, and to ask what exactly it is caring about right now.
fear.practice: Finish the sentence: “I'm afraid for…” — and look at what comes after the dots. Most likely, it is something truly dear to you.

sadness.text: Sadness has a right to exist, even without a clear cause. For Heidegger we are never “without a mood”: even grey indifference is a mood. A mood, he wrote, comes neither from outside nor from inside but rises out of our very “being-in-the-world”; we don't choose it, we find ourselves in it. So sadness is not a dark pane of glass between you and reality, but one of the ways reality discloses itself at all: in sadness, fragility, silence and what is passing become more visible. Merleau-Ponty would show how sadness changes perception itself: colours fade, steps grow heavy, the world seems to recede. This isn't deception but an honest bodily language. Sadness doesn't have to be fixed urgently — you can let it show you what it sees.
sadness.practice: Look around for a minute and note: what do you notice now, in sadness, that you usually don't?

grief.text: Grief is one of the deepest human attunements, and it needs no justification. Heidegger observed that we can't experience another person's death “from the inside” — we remain nearby, in mourning, care and memory. The one who is gone hasn't simply vanished: they are still part of your world — that shared world which, for Heidegger, we always inhabit with others (he called this “being-with,” Mitsein). Hence the pain: the world is being rearranged, and familiar paths lead to an empty place. Merleau-Ponty would add that the body remembers: hands, habits, everyday routes keep the presence of the one who is gone. From this point of view, grief is not an illness but a form of faithfulness to a bond. It doesn't need to be “got through faster”; the world can rearrange itself slowly, keeping a place for what was lost.
grief.practice: Recall one bodily habit connected with the person or thing you've lost. Just notice it, without changing or judging anything.

loneliness.text: Loneliness is painful, and there's nothing shameful about it. Heidegger held that human beings are essentially “being-with” (Mitsein): we always already live in a world shared with others. So, as he saw it, even loneliness is a particular way of being with others: you can only miss someone who in principle could be there. Your loneliness isn't proof that you're built “wrong” but evidence that you're made for connection. Merleau-Ponty spoke of “intercorporeality” — the way bodies understand one another even before words: through a glance, a gesture, an intonation. Perhaps loneliness is the body's longing for this kind of living response. To accept it is to hear in it not a verdict but a direction.
loneliness.practice: Recall one recent moment of living response — even just a glance or a smile from a stranger. What exactly happened between you then?

anger.text: Anger is a living feeling, and it often speaks of something important. Heidegger hardly wrote about anger directly, but from the standpoint of his analysis of attunement we might say: in anger, the world appears as something that affects us, that “concerns” us. What is indifferent to us doesn't make us angry; so anger, too, is a form of “care.” Merleau-Ponty would draw attention to the body: anger isn't a thought to which sensations were later added, but a whole way of being in a situation — tension, heat, readiness to act. The body “understood” what was happening as a violation before you had time to put it into words. To accept anger is not to be ashamed of it but to ask: what boundary, what value is it protecting right now?
anger.practice: Place your palm where you feel the anger most strongly in your body and ask: “What matters to me here?”

shame.text: Shame is one of the most painful feelings, and everyone knows it. Merleau-Ponty described the body as something that both sees and is seen: we don't just look at the world, we can always find ourselves under someone else's gaze. Shame is the moment when the body suddenly feels exposed, turned into an object, and you want to disappear. Heidegger would add the concept of “das Man” — the impersonal “they,” “the done thing”: often we're ashamed not before a specific person but before an anonymous “that's not how it's done.” From this point of view you can ask: whose standard is this — your own, or “people in general”? Shame doesn't make you worse; it shows how much it matters to you to be among others. And sometimes it's enough to notice that this gaze is not yet the whole world.
shame.practice: Ask yourself: “Before whom exactly am I ashamed — a specific person, or an impersonal ‘what will people say’?”

guilt.text: Guilt is heavy, but it doesn't make you a bad person. Heidegger distinguished everyday guilt — a debt, a wrongdoing — from a deeper “being-guilty” (Schuldigsein), which, as he saw it, belongs to human beings as such. In choosing one thing, we inevitably don't choose another; we can't do everything, and we never begin with a clean slate. To be human is to be finite and always to fall short somewhere. This is not a verdict but a release from the illusion of flawlessness. The “call of conscience,” for Heidegger, commands nothing specific and makes no accusations — it simply brings you back to your own life. You can listen to guilt, put right what really can be put right, and let go of the demand to be infinite.
guilt.practice: Divide a sheet into two columns: “what I can actually put right” and “what is simply part of my finitude.” Look at the second one gently.

envy.text: Envy is unpleasant, but it's an ordinary human feeling. Heidegger described everyday life as absorption in “das Man” — the impersonal “they”: we constantly compare ourselves, find out how “everyone” lives and measure ourselves by other people's yardsticks. He called this “distantiality” (Abständigkeit) — a quiet, almost imperceptible preoccupation with the distance between ourselves and others. From this point of view, you might say envy is a sign that for a while you're seeing your own life through someone else's eyes. But it also holds a clue: envy points to what you want. Heidegger spoke of “authenticity” (Eigentlichkeit) — a life you understand as your own, not as a copy of a common template. Then envy becomes not a reproach but a question: what do I want — not “they”?
envy.practice: Name what you envy, and rephrase it as “I would like…”. Does your wish match what the other person has?

emptiness.text: Emptiness and apathy are very hard states, and they deserve gentleness, not reproach. Heidegger described moments when things stop calling to us and meaning anything, and everything “becomes indifferent.” For him such states are not just a glitch: in them something usually hidden shows through — that the world as a whole rests on our involvement. He spoke of “the Nothing” (das Nichts) not as a catastrophe but as the background against which anything can become important at all. Merleau-Ponty would remind us that meaning is born in the body and in movement, in the simplest gestures. Sometimes the way out of emptiness begins not with a big idea but with a small bodily contact with the world: a warm cup, footsteps, a sound. Emptiness is not a final answer but a world that has gone quiet for a while.
emptiness.practice: Choose one simple sensation right now — the warmth of your palms, the support under your feet — and stay with it for half a minute, demanding nothing of yourself.

confusion.text: Confusion is an honest reaction to a world that has stopped making sense. Heidegger described how we usually live “absorbed in our dealings”: things are “ready-to-hand” (zuhanden) for us — we use them without thinking, like a hammer in the hand. Only when something breaks does the thing suddenly become noticeable and strange. Confusion is like such a breakdown of the familiar: what used to work “by itself” has stopped working. It's unpleasant, but that's exactly when the very structure of your life, usually invisible, comes into view. Heidegger also spoke of “thrownness” (Geworfenheit): we always find ourselves in a situation we didn't choose — and that isn't your fault. Confusion is not a failure but a moment when you can take a fresh look at what matters to you.
confusion.practice: Write one sentence: “What exactly has stopped working ‘by itself’?” Don't look for a solution yet — just name it.

fatigue.text: Fatigue is not laziness or weakness but the language of the body. Merleau-Ponty showed that the body is not a tool operated by the mind but our way of being in the world: it is through the body that we have a world at all. At the root of our experience he saw a bodily “I can” — the ability to reach, to walk, to take something on. When the body is tired, the world literally changes: distances grow longer, tasks heavier, “I can” turns into “I can't.” Heidegger would add that in constant busyness we easily dissolve into our tasks and into the impersonal “it must be done,” forgetting ourselves. From this point of view, fatigue is not an enemy to defeat but a signal of your embodied existence: you are not a machine, and your world has the right to become smaller for a while so that you can recover.
fatigue.practice: Ask your body, not your mind: “What do you want right now?” — and note the first answer, even if it's very simple.

quote.text: I am not in front of my body, I am in it, or rather I am it.
quote.author: Maurice Merleau-Ponty

boredom.text: Boredom seems trivial, but Heidegger devoted a large part of his lecture course The Fundamental Concepts of Metaphysics (1929–1930) to it. He distinguished superficial boredom — at a railway station waiting for a train, say — from “profound boredom,” when everything at once becomes indifferent, including ourselves. In profound boredom time seems to stand still, and we find ourselves facing what we usually drown out with constant busyness. For Heidegger this is not a waste of life but one of the “fundamental moods,” which can awaken a question: what do I actually want to live for? Boredom doesn't have to be filled with something right away. You can give it a little space — and see what it opens up.
boredom.practice: Next time you're bored, wait two minutes before picking up your phone. What surfaces in that pause?

quote.text: Profound boredom, drifting here and there in the abysses of our existence like a muffling fog, removes all things and human beings and oneself along with them into a remarkable indifference.
quote.author: Martin Heidegger

joy.text: Joy is as real a knowledge of the world as anxiety is. In his lecture “What Is Metaphysics?”, Heidegger gives joy in the presence of someone we love as a mood in which “beings as a whole” are revealed to us. In other words, joy is not a superficial emotion but a way in which the world suddenly appears whole, close and open. Merleau-Ponty would show how joy changes the body: it becomes light, movements become free, everything seems within reach. This is the bodily “I can” at its fullest. To accept joy is not to devalue it with thoughts like “this won't last” or “I don't deserve it,” but to let it be a full experience of the world. Joy needs no justification and doesn't have to “pay for itself.”
joy.practice: Where in your body do you feel joy? Keep your attention there for three calm breaths — just so the joy is noticed.

love.text: Love and tenderness are among the deepest ways of being with another. Speaking of “caring for another” (Fürsorge), Heidegger distinguished two extreme forms. One, as it were, leaps in and takes over the other's concerns, quietly making them dependent. The other “leaps ahead” of them — and gives their own care back to them, helping them become themselves. From this point of view, mature tenderness is closer to the second, liberating form. Merleau-Ponty would show that love begins in the body: in a touch, the one “touching” and the one “touched” intertwine, and the boundary between “I” and “you” becomes permeable. To love is to be vulnerable, and there's no weakness in that. Tenderness is a bodily knowledge of the other, and it can be trusted.
love.practice: Recall how exactly your tenderness shows itself — a gesture, a tone, a touch. Which is there more of: care that acts “instead of” the other, or care that sets them free?

gratitude.text: Gratitude is a warm and important feeling. In his late lectures What Is Called Thinking? (1951–1952), Heidegger brought together the German words denken (“to think”) and danken (“to thank”): genuine thinking, as he saw it, is akin to gratitude — an attentive receiving of what is given to us. From this point of view, gratitude is not a polite formula but a way of seeing: things are not to be taken for granted; they are given to us. Merleau-Ponty would add that we receive the world from the very start — through the body, perception, language, other people — before we ever do anything ourselves. Gratitude, then, is an acknowledgement of our rootedness in the world. It doesn't have to be earned or turned into a debt; you can simply let it be.
gratitude.practice: Name one thing in today that you usually take for granted, and say to yourself: “This was given to me.”

hope.text: Hope faces the future, and it is legitimate even when a lot is unclear. Heidegger believed human beings are by nature directed forward: he called this “being-ahead-of-itself.” We always already live in our possibilities, not only in what is here now. For Heidegger a person is not a set of fixed properties but a “potentiality-for-being” (Seinkönnen), an open space of what they may yet become. He also wrote about the finitude of life — but for him the understanding that time is not endless makes life not less valuable but more: it brings us back to what really matters. From this point of view, hope is an expression of the fact that you are a being of possibilities. You can cherish it without demanding guarantees from it.
hope.practice: Write three times: “I am someone for whom it is still possible to…” The answers can be very small.

nostalgia.text: Nostalgia is a tender ache for the past, and it says a lot about you. Heidegger emphasised that for a human being the past is not simply what has gone and finished. He called it “having-been-ness” (Gewesenheit): our past goes on living in us and shapes how we see the present and what we expect from the future. We are “thrown” into a history, a language, a family, traditions, and we carry them with us. Merleau-Ponty would show how the past is kept in the body: a smell, a tune or a taste suddenly brings back a whole world — that's bodily memory, not just thought. From this point of view, nostalgia is not an escape from life but a meeting with what made you. You can accept it as a grateful look back from which to draw strength.
nostalgia.practice: Recall one sensory memory — a smell, a sound, a taste. What from that time would you like to take with you into today?

craving.text: A craving is a sharp “I want it right now,” and there's nothing shameful in it: this is how the body and habit pull us towards a familiar relief. In Being and Time, Heidegger briefly examines “urge” and “addiction” (Drang, Hang) as modifications of “care” — our constant involvement in the world. From this point of view, you might say that in addiction the world narrows: of all possibilities only one remains, and it seems to pull you towards itself. Merleau-Ponty would add that a craving lives in the body before thought: the hand, the breath, the gaze are already turned towards the object. So a craving is not your “true desire” and not a verdict, but a wave of bodily attunement. Like any attunement, it rises, peaks and changes. You can notice it without arguing with it or giving in straight away — and watch the world gradually widen again.
craving.practice: Describe the craving as a bodily sensation: where is it in your body, what is it like — warm, tight, pulsing? Watch for a couple of minutes how its strength changes.

addiction.text: Addiction is not a moral failure or a “weakness of character.” Merleau-Ponty wrote a great deal about habit: as he saw it, a habit is not a mechanical reflex but knowledge that lives in the body, a way of inhabiting the world. A typist doesn't remember where the letters are on the keyboard — the fingers know by themselves. In the same way, a long-standing cycle of addiction becomes written into the body, into the daily routine, into routes, into what an evening or a Friday looks like. From Heidegger's point of view, you might say the whole world becomes “attuned” around one thing: objects and hours take on meaning in relation to it. This explains why getting out is so hard: it isn't one habit that changes but a whole world. But hope follows from the same thought: since the body once learned, it can also relearn — slowly, through repetition, with the support of others. It's a path, not a single decision.
addiction.practice: Note one place or time of day that is especially “attuned” to the familiar cycle. What is the smallest thing you could rearrange in it today?

hangover.text: A hangover is doubly hard: the body aches, and in the morning anxiety, shame and fragments of the evening that won't fit together come up. This state deserves gentleness, not a verdict. Merleau-Ponty showed that in ordinary life the body is “transparent”: we live through it without noticing — we look with our eyes, not at them. In a hangover the body suddenly comes to the foreground — heavy, alien, demanding attention — and the world around seems dull and prickly too. Gaps in memory add to the anxiety: as if part of your own time were hidden from you. Heidegger would remind us that attunement colours everything at once — last night, yourself and the future. From this point of view, the morning gloom is not the final truth about you but a mood that will pass. Meanwhile, you can simply look after the body that is so noticeable right now.
hangover.practice: Do one simple kind thing for your body — fresh air, a warm shower, an unhurried meal — and notice how it responds.

euphoria.text: A burst of euphoria is a real experience, and there's no need to suspect it straight away. Heidegger wrote that an “elated mood” can lift from us the familiar burden of being — the load we usually carry without noticing. In such moments the world opens up differently: distances shrink, everything seems attainable, the future wide open. For a phenomenologist this is not an illusion but one of the ways the world can be given to us at all. Merleau-Ponty would add that the high is felt in the body: lightness in movement, fast speech, the wish to embrace everything at once. Understanding this is useful not to spoil the moment but to live it attentively: to remember how the world looks in this light, and to notice which of the possibilities that have opened up you'll still want to test on a calm morning.
euphoria.practice: Write in one line how the world looks right now and what seems possible. Reread it later, in an ordinary mood — just to compare.

crash.text: The drop after a high — after a celebration, a success, or something that lifted you for a while — can be very hard, and it isn't your fault. Heidegger wrote that in our moods the “burdensome” character of existence is disclosed to us one way or another: life has to be carried. An elated mood lifts this burden for a while but doesn't cancel it; when the high goes, the weight is felt more sharply, by contrast. What matters is that the crash, too, is an attunement, not the final truth about the world. A mood, for Heidegger, can't simply be switched off by an act of will — it can only be changed by another, counter-mood. And that comes not through force but through the body and simple tasks. Merleau-Ponty would remind us: the world comes back to us through movement — a step, a breath, a look out of the window.
crash.practice: Without demanding a lift from yourself, make one simple movement — stretch, walk around the room, open a window — and notice what has changed, even by one percent.

panic.text: Panic is one of the most frightening experiences: your heart pounds, your breath falters, it seems that something irreparable is about to happen. This fear is real, and you're not exaggerating anything. Heidegger described how in intense fear a person “loses their head”: attention darts from one thing to another, holding on to nothing, and the familiar world seems to fall apart. Merleau-Ponty showed that our “I” is first of all bodily: we find ourselves through the support of our feet, the position of our hands, the boundaries of our skin. In panic this support seems to slip away. So the phenomenological answer is simple and bodily: don't argue with your thoughts, but bring the world back to yourself through the body — through what you can feel and name. A wave of panic usually peaks and subsides within a few minutes; a body that feels the floor underfoot helps you wait it out.
panic.practice: Put both feet on the floor and feel the support. Take a few breaths with the exhale longer than the inhale, and name out loud five objects you can see around you.

dread.text: Existential dread — when the question “what's the point of it all?” suddenly opens up and the abyss of finitude comes into view — is one of the hardest experiences. Heidegger didn't consider it a sickness of the mind. In his lecture “What Is Metaphysics?” he wrote that in anxiety all beings seem to slip away — and that it is precisely then that the fundamental wonder first arises: why are there beings at all, rather than nothing? He also stressed that knowing our finitude makes life truly our own. You might say: since time is not endless, every “now” has weight and won't come again. From this point of view, dread is the other side of wonder that the world and you exist at all. This question doesn't need to be solved tonight. You can let it be — and notice that you're asking it as someone alive, in a living world.
dread.practice: Write down one thing near you that is astonishing simply because it exists: light, a sound, someone's face, your own breathing.

fomo.text: The fear of missing out is very understandable: the feed shows others living more vividly, and you seem to be in the wrong place. Heidegger described this long before social media. “Curiosity” (Neugier), in his analysis, is not a thirst to understand but an urge to see the new for the sake of novelty: it jumps from one thing to the next and never lingers anywhere. He called this “never dwelling anywhere” (Aufenthaltslosigkeit): being everywhere and nowhere at once. And “idle talk” (Gerede) creates the feeling that everyone already knows where real life is, and it's somewhere out there. This is the anonymous voice of “the they” (das Man) — not anyone's specific opinion but an impersonal “this is how people live.” From this point of view, FOMO is not a sign that your life is worse but a trace of a scattered gaze. Its opposite is lingering: life happens where you actually are.
fomo.practice: Choose one thing near you and linger on it for two minutes — look at it as if for the first time. What did you notice that you hadn't seen before?

sleepless.text: Insomnia and three-in-the-morning thoughts are exhausting, and being annoyed with yourself only adds weight. In the Phenomenology of Perception, Merleau-Ponty described precisely how sleep comes. I lie down, close my eyes, breathe slowly, imitating a sleeper — and at some point the imitation becomes real: sleep “comes,” just as in the ancient mysteries the god appeared to those who acted out scenes from his life. Sleep can't be seized by will; it can only be invited by the body. And night-time thoughts, from Heidegger's point of view, can be understood as a particular attunement: in the dark, when nothing can be done, the world shrinks to worries, and each one seems huge. In the morning the same thought often weighs something different. So there's no need to argue with night-time conclusions — it's enough not to take them as final and to let the body play the part of the sleeper.
sleepless.practice: Lie down comfortably and “play” a sleeper: relax your face, slow your breathing, make the exhale longer. Don't wait for sleep — just play the part.

betrayal.text: Betrayal is one of the deepest wounds, and the pain it causes makes sense. Heidegger wrote that we always already live in a world shared with others (Mitsein), and much of this world rests on the “taken for granted” — on trust we don't notice, the way we don't notice the floor under our feet. Betrayal wounds more than feelings: it breaks this unnoticed background, and suddenly everything familiar is called into question — past conversations, shared memories, your own capacity to trust. Merleau-Ponty would add that trust is bodily: it lives in relaxed shoulders next to a person, in the habit of turning towards them. That's why betrayal feels almost like a blow. From this point of view, your bewilderment is not naivety but evidence of how genuine your openness was.
betrayal.practice: Name one person or one place where your trust is still intact. Stay for a minute with this feeling of support.

jealousy.text: Jealousy is agonising, and very many people know it. Merleau-Ponty stressed that another person is only ever given to us from one side. I see their face and gestures, hear their words, but their world, their perception, their life from the inside I can never live for them. This isn't a flaw in the relationship but the very condition of encounter: the other is not an object but a different point of view on the world. Jealousy can be understood as a painful encounter with this irremovable separateness: you want the person you love to have no side hidden from you. Heidegger would add that jealousy is an attunement in which the whole world is coloured by a single question, and any trifle becomes a sign. From this point of view, there's no need to be ashamed of jealousy: it carries a longing for closeness — and the pain of knowing that closeness doesn't cancel the other's freedom.
jealousy.practice: Recall a moment when someone close to you revealed an unexpected side of themselves — and it was good. Let yourself notice that their separateness can also bring joy.

resentment.text: An old grievance is heavy: you carry it for years, and it doesn't seem to be going anywhere. There's no weakness in this — it means something truly mattered to you. Heidegger believed the past doesn't stay behind us like a station we've passed: we are our “having-been” (Gewesenheit); it keeps sounding in the present and in how we await the future. Merleau-Ponty showed that the past settles in the body: in a clenched jaw at the sound of a name, in wariness, in habitual protective gestures. You might say resentment is the past that has stayed present because the wound was never acknowledged. From this point of view, you don't have to force yourself to “let it go.” To begin with, you can acknowledge it and notice where it lives in your body. Pain that has been acknowledged gradually stops being the only way of remembering.
resentment.practice: Recall the grievance and ask yourself: where is it in my body right now? Place your palm there and take a few calm breaths out.

heartbreak.text: A broken heart is real pain, and there's no need to be ashamed of how strongly you feel it. Merleau-Ponty examined the “phantom limb” in detail: a person who has lost an arm goes on feeling it for a long time, because the body is still directed towards a world in which that arm was needed. From this point of view, a break-up can be understood too. Your body and your habits still live in the shared world: your hand reaches for the phone, your eyes look for a familiar silhouette, your evening is still arranged for two out of habit. Heidegger would add that the whole world changes along with the person: songs, streets and smells take on a different meaning. That's why a break-up hurts for so long: the world doesn't rearrange itself in a day. This isn't “clinging to the past” but the slow work of a body and a world learning to live anew.
heartbreak.practice: Notice one habit that is still “waiting” for the other person. Don't scold yourself for it — just gently name it: “my body still remembers.”

impostor.text: The feeling that you're about to be found out is very common, and it often visits precisely the conscientious. Heidegger described the anonymous authority of “the they” (das Man): “this is how it's done,” “this is what's expected,” “real professionals don't make mistakes like that.” No one in particular stands behind this voice, but we measure ourselves by it without meaning to. Impostor syndrome can be understood as comparing yourself from the inside — with all your doubts — to faceless “them” on the outside, who seemingly have no doubts. But “they” have no inner life: they are an abstraction. Every real person also learns as they go and also doubts. Merleau-Ponty would add that skill lives in the body and in practice, not in a feeling of confidence: your hands often know more than your head is ready to admit.
impostor.practice: Write down one concrete thing you're good at — not as an evaluation but as a fact: “this is something I can do.”

self_hatred.text: Self-hatred and a merciless inner critic are a very hard state, and you deserve gentleness, not yet another verdict. Heidegger has the concept of “the call of conscience,” and it helps to distinguish something important. The genuine call, for Heidegger, lists nothing and brands no one: it silently calls a person to their own possibilities, to being themselves. He considered the everyday understanding of conscience as a ledger of wrongdoings a distortion of it. And the voice that insists “you're worthless” more often speaks the language of “the they” (das Man) — other people's yardsticks, judgements and comparisons, absorbed at some point. It is loud, but it isn't your deepest voice. From this point of view, its verdict is not the truth about you. Beneath it there is another, quiet call — not to punishment, but to life.
self_hatred.practice: Write down one sentence from your inner critic and ask: “Whose voice is saying this? Where have I heard it before?” Just notice the answer.

helplessness.text: Helplessness is a very heavy feeling, when it seems that nothing depends on you. Heidegger spoke of “thrownness” (Geworfenheit): we always already find ourselves in a situation we didn't choose — in a body, in a history, in circumstances. This is not your fault but a shared human condition. Merleau-Ponty described the body as a primary “I can”: the world for us is a field of what we can reach, what we can pick up, where we can go. In helplessness this “I can” seems to shrink to a point. But it doesn't vanish completely: even in the tightest situation something remains within reach — straightening a pillow, opening a window, writing one word. From this point of view, you don't have to change everything at once. You can begin by giving your body back at least a small “I can.”
helplessness.practice: Find one very small action within arm's reach and do it slowly, noticing: “I managed that.”

procrastination.text: “I can't get started” is a familiar and agonising state, and it almost never comes down to laziness. Heidegger observed that we understand the world first of all not with an observer's eyes but in dealing with things: a tool is truly understood when you work with it, not when you think about it. While a task stays in your head, it seems huge and shapeless — a whole “project” you look at from the outside. Merleau-Ponty would add that the body understands a task once it starts moving: fingers on the keyboard, an open notebook, a tool in your hand already suggest the next step. From this point of view, you can begin not with resolve but with touch: not “do everything,” but simply pick the thing up. Understanding often comes along the way.
procrastination.practice: Without starting the work, just prepare it with your body: open the file, put the pen on the page, pick up the tool. Stay like that for a minute — with no obligation to go on.

uprooted.text: Being cut off from home is a deep experience: after a move or emigration the ground seems to slip from under your feet, and this is no whim. Merleau-Ponty showed that space for us is not a map but a lived-in world: the body knows where the light switch is, how to get to the shop, how your native language sounds. In a new place all this has to be learned again, and the body feels like a stranger for a long time. Heidegger thought a great deal about “dwelling” (Wohnen): for him, to live is not just to be somewhere but to inhabit a place with care. He considered the loss of such rootedness not only a personal fate but the shared fate of modern people. From this point of view, your sense of being lost is not a failure but an honest response to the loss of a lived-in world. Home is not just an address: it grows again out of habits, routes and people.
uprooted.practice: Choose one small spot in the new place — a bench, a café, a route — and start returning to it. Feeling at home begins with repetition.

quote.text: Homelessness is coming to be the destiny of the world.
quote.author: Martin Heidegger

overload.text: Overload and the endless feed are exhausting, and it's not that you're “not coping.” The late Heidegger wrote about “enframing” (Gestell) — an arrangement of the technological world in which everything, including human beings and their attention, becomes a resource to be used. A stream of notifications is a good illustration: it demands a reaction constantly. Yet Heidegger didn't call for throwing technology away. In his address “Releasement” (Gelassenheit) he proposed saying both “yes” and “no” to technical things at once: using them, but not letting them take hold of us entirely. From this point of view, being tired of the noise is a healthy response: something in you resists being turned into a resource. You can allow yourself small islands of releasement, where things once again mean something in themselves.
overload.practice: Put your phone face down for two minutes and look at one thing in the room as if it didn't need to be photographed or rated.

unreality.text: The feeling that everything around you, or you yourself, isn't quite real is a strange and often frightening experience, and it's hard to put into words. Merleau-Ponty called our ordinary certainty about the world “perceptual faith”: before any proof, we live with the sense that things exist, that they're solid and real. This faith rests not on logic but on the body — so sometimes it can weaken, as if a pane of glass had appeared between you and the world. Phenomenology begins precisely where what is usually unnoticed becomes noticeable: an experience like this, however hard, shows how finely woven our connection with the world is. Merleau-Ponty stressed that this connection lives in sensation — in touch, weight, temperature, sound. The world answers the body before it answers the mind.
unreality.practice: Pick up an object with a distinct texture — a cool cup, a rough piece of fabric — and describe out loud to yourself its weight, temperature and surface.

awe.text: Awe before something vast or beautiful — mountains, the sea, the night sky, music — is one of the most precious experiences. Heidegger considered wonder one of the original moods from which thought itself is born: the Greeks already said that philosophy begins in wonder. In awe the world is not simply perceived but appears in all its unexpected givenness — as if it were being shown for the first time. Merleau-Ponty saw the task of philosophy as giving us back this fresh gaze, hidden behind habit. He loved the painting of Cézanne, who, as he saw it, tried to paint the world at the moment of its birth, before it hardened into ready-made forms. From this point of view, awe is not fleeting sentimentality but a moment when seeing becomes clear. You can simply allow yourself to have it.
awe.practice: Stay with whatever filled you with awe for another minute, without photographing or describing it. Just let it be bigger than you.

quote.text: True philosophy consists in relearning to look at the world.
quote.author: Maurice Merleau-Ponty

relief.text: Relief is one of the most blessed sensations, and it's worth living through without hurrying. From Heidegger's point of view, every mood discloses the world in its own way, and relief is especially telling: only when the weight is lifted do we really see how much we were carrying. The world becomes spacious again, the future open. Merleau-Ponty would draw attention to the body: relief is almost always bodily — the shoulders drop, the breath deepens, the face smooths out. This is the body returning to a world from which tension had pushed it out. So relief is not a trifle after which you must rush straight on, but a moment when body and world find each other again. Let it last: notice it while it's here.
relief.practice: Notice where in your body you feel the relief — in your shoulders, your breathing, your belly. Take one slow breath out, as if confirming: “yes, it's easier now.”

calm.text: Calm and peace are precious states, and they don't need to be earned or justified. In a short text, “The Pathway” (1949), Heidegger described a path across the fields that he had walked since childhood: an old oak, a wooden bench, the changing seasons. Such a path, he wrote, teaches something simple — what remains when the bustle dies down. For Heidegger, calm is not emptiness or inaction but a special openness: things stop being tasks and become simply things again. Merleau-Ponty would add that calm is felt in the body as agreement with the rhythm of the world: breath falls in with your step, your gaze is in no hurry. From this point of view, calm is not an absence of life but life that doesn't need to prove its worth. You can simply allow it to yourself.
calm.practice: Sit comfortably and watch for a couple of minutes how the things around you simply are — a chair, light, a wall — asking nothing of them or of yourself.

inspiration.text: Inspiration is a joyful and mysterious state, and it's worth cherishing. In the essay “Eye and Mind,” Merleau-Ponty wrote that the painter changes the world into paintings “by lending his body to the world”: inspiration is not a thought handed down from above but an exchange between the body and the world. He cited the painter André Marchand, who more than once felt in a forest that it was not he who was looking at the trees, but the trees that were looking at him. Heidegger, too, believed that genuine creation is more a listening than a manufacturing: in a work of art, the world seems to open itself up. From this point of view, inspiration is neither a merit nor an accident but a moment when you are especially open to what surrounds you. There's no need to hold on to it by force: you can simply follow it and pay attention to what it shows you.
inspiration.practice: Don't write down the whole idea — just the first image or phrase that came. Let it be a beginning, not a finished result.

schadenfreude.text: Schadenfreude is a feeling that's awkward to notice in yourself, but it's very human. In Being and Time, Heidegger describes how, living among others, we are constantly and almost unknowingly preoccupied with our distance from them: are we falling behind, catching up, getting ahead? He called this feature of everyday “being-with-others” distantiality. From this point of view, you might say schadenfreude is a flash of relief within this endless comparing: someone else's fall shrinks, for a moment, the distance that was tormenting us. It's less malice than weariness with the comparison we're all drawn into. Once you notice this, you can loosen your grip a little: your life doesn't have to be measured by its distance from others.
schadenfreude.practice: Ask yourself: “Whom am I always measuring my distance against?” Imagine for a minute that this ruler doesn't exist.

contempt.text: Contempt is a cold feeling, and it isn't easy to admit it in yourself. Don't rush to judge yourself. Heidegger described our relation to others as “solicitude” and noted that in everyday life it mostly exists in “deficient” modes: we pass each other by; the other “doesn't concern us.” Merleau-Ponty would add that we perceive another person first of all with the body — through gestures, gait, intonation — and understand them long before we have time to think. From this point of view, you might say contempt is a way of pushing someone away, making them “none of my concern,” most often because something in them did touch us after all. Ask not “who is this person?” but “what in me responded to their gesture?”
contempt.practice: Recall exactly which gesture, tone or act made you feel contempt. Name what it touched in you.

disgust.text: Disgust is a very bodily feeling, and it has every right to exist. Merleau-Ponty showed that the body doesn't simply pass sensations on to consciousness but itself “understands” the world: it knows at once what to reach for and what to recoil from, before any reasoning. Disgust is one such instant bodily meaning. When it's aimed at a situation or at people, it's the body saying “I can't be here.” When it's aimed at yourself, perhaps you're looking at your body from the outside, as an object, rather than living in it. Merleau-Ponty distinguished the “object-body,” which is looked at, from the “lived body,” through which we live. From this point of view, you can return to your body from the inside, rather than only judging it from the outside.
disgust.practice: Close your eyes and feel your feet, your palms, your breathing from the inside — not how you look, but how you are. For one minute.

revenge.text: The wish for revenge is understandable: you've been hurt, and a force rises inside demanding justice. In his lecture “Who Is Nietzsche's Zarathustra?”, Heidegger examines Nietzsche's idea of the “spirit of revenge.” On his reading, revenge at bottom is the will's aversion to time and its “it was”: we can't change the past, and this powerlessness looks for an outlet by taking itself out on someone. From this point of view, the wish for revenge is not cruelty but torment over a past that can't be undone. This helps you see that no revenge will undo what happened. But you can look for ways to live with that “it was”: protecting yourself, seeking justice, giving the pain time.
revenge.practice: Write: “What I can least accept is that this happened…” Just name it, without trying to fix it.

anger_at_loved.text: Anger at those close to you — a partner, parents, children — is familiar to almost everyone, as is the shame that follows. You're not a bad person. Heidegger wrote that a mood “assails” us: we don't choose it, we find ourselves in it, and it colours the whole world. Often we bring home a mood that formed somewhere else — and then any small thing a loved one does flares up in that light. Merleau-Ponty would add that with family we live in a shared bodily space: their movements, voices and habits constantly touch us, and a tired body reacts before we have time to think. From this point of view, an outburst is not the truth about your love but about your mood and your tiredness.
anger_at_loved.practice: After an outburst, ask: “What mood was I in before this even happened?” Name it in one word.

ambivalence.text: Loving someone and at the same time not being able to stand them is hard, but very human. Merleau-Ponty's philosophy is sometimes called a “philosophy of ambiguity.” He showed that ambiguity is not an error of thinking but the very fabric of experience: our body both sees and is seen, we are both inside the world and looking at it, meaning is never finally clear. Heidegger, for his part, believed that care for another can take different forms, and they often intertwine. From this point of view, mixed feelings towards someone close are not a sign of fake love but the natural many-sidedness of living relationships. You don't have to untangle the knot right away. You can simply acknowledge that it's there.
ambivalence.practice: Say out loud: “I love you, and it's hard for me to be with you.” Notice how it sounds in your body when both parts are true.

guilty_relief.text: Relief after a break-up, a departure or a loved one's long illness can bring guilt. But relief doesn't cancel love. Heidegger wrote that moods disclose our existence to us as a “burden”: life doesn't simply go on; it has to be carried. When you carried someone else's illness, a difficult relationship, sleepless nights for a long time, that burden wasn't a metaphor but your everyday being. From this point of view, relief is not betrayal but simply a change in the mood through which the world is disclosed: the weight has eased, and the body has felt it. Merleau-Ponty would remind us that the body knows its tiredness before our thoughts do. You can allow yourself both to breathe out and to grieve — one doesn't cancel the other.
guilty_relief.practice: Sit comfortably and feel where in your body things have become lighter. Tell yourself: “I carried a lot. I'm allowed to breathe out.”

indifference.text: Sometimes, where something “should” move you, there's silence inside. That's frightening, but it doesn't make you heartless. In Being and Time, Heidegger noticed something remarkable: even a flat, colourless lack of mood, when nothing touches you, is also a mood, not an absence of feeling. We are always attuned somehow; it's just that sometimes the mood is grey and quiet. And it, too, discloses something: tiredness, for example, or that the world has moved back for a while. From this point of view, indifference is not a hole in you but the way the world is given to you right now. You don't have to force yourself to feel “correctly.” You can describe this silence attentively, and describing it sometimes changes it by itself.
indifference.practice: Describe your indifference in three words, like the weather: what colour, weight and temperature is it?

escape.text: The urge to drop everything and leave — your job, your city, your role — says a lot in itself. Heidegger described how in everyday life we live by an impersonal “the done thing,” and this can quietly obscure our own possibilities. Sometimes, he wrote, a “call of conscience” sounds — not the voice of morality, but a quiet summons back to yourself, to what you actually could be. From this point of view, you might say the urge to run away isn't necessarily flight from yourself; sometimes it is exactly such a call. But it rarely demands that you destroy everything at once. Heidegger spoke of “projecting” possibilities: first you can simply see them and look at them closely.
escape.practice: Write: “What part of me can't be seen in my current role?” Don't decide anything — just take a close look.

forbidden_attraction.text: Attraction to someone who is “off-limits” can be unsettling and frightening. But the feeling itself decides nothing yet and doesn't make you bad. Merleau-Ponty showed that desire is not simply a thought or an instinct but a way the body is turned towards the world and towards another: it creates a particular atmosphere and gives a person a significance that's hard to put into words. Such meaning arises before reasoning, so we can't simply “cancel” it by deciding to. From this point of view, you can approach the attraction with curiosity: what exactly does this person open up for you — aliveness, recognition, another version of yourself? Understanding the meaning of a feeling doesn't mean acting on it. It means knowing your own life better.
forbidden_attraction.practice: Write down what the world becomes when you think of this person: brighter, more anxious, freer? One word.

social_anxiety.text: Fear of people and their judgement is an exhausting feeling, and you're not alone in it. Heidegger described the impersonal “das Man” — “the they,” “the done thing”: an anonymous authority that tells you how to look, talk and carry yourself. Often we're afraid not of a specific person but of this invisible “everyone.” Merleau-Ponty would add that under another's gaze the body stiffens: movements that usually flow by themselves suddenly have to be thought through. From this point of view, your shyness is an understandable bodily reaction to anonymous judgement. But Heidegger noted that this “everyone” is no one in particular. Sometimes it helps to come back from “what will people think” to the specific person in front of you, who is most likely a little nervous too.
social_anxiety.practice: Before a meeting, replace the thought “what will everyone think” with the question: “Who exactly will be there — and what do I know about them?”

quote.text: Everyone is the other, and no one is himself.
quote.author: Martin Heidegger

uncertainty.text: Uncertainty is draining: you want something to hold on to, and there's nothing. Heidegger described the human situation through two concepts. “Thrownness”: we have always already landed in a situation we didn't choose and can't fully survey. “Projection”: we live on nonetheless, reaching towards possibilities without knowing for sure which will come true. From this point of view, uncertainty is not a malfunction but the basic structure of life, usually obscured by familiar plans. Merleau-Ponty added a consolation: however unclear the world is, we can't be left entirely without meaning — it keeps taking shape in our experience. You don't have to wait for complete clarity; you can look for meaning in the next small step.
uncertainty.practice: Name one thing you're sure of right now — even the simplest: the cup in your hand, the floor under your feet.

quote.text: Because we are in the world, we are condemned to meaning.
quote.author: Maurice Merleau-Ponty

waiting.text: Waiting — for results, an answer, news — can stretch out agonisingly. In the conversation “Towards an Explication of Releasement,” the late Heidegger distinguished two kinds of waiting. One is a tense awaiting of something definite: we fasten onto the future, and the present becomes an empty corridor. The other is an open waiting that doesn't cling to a particular outcome and lets things come as they will. He linked this stance with “releasement” — a calm allowing of what is not in our power. From this point of view, what makes waiting agonising is often that we hold the future too tightly. Without ceasing to hope, you can loosen your grip a little and notice what is happening now.
waiting.practice: Unclench your fists, drop your shoulders, and for three minutes simply listen to the sounds around you, expecting nothing from them.

regret.text: Regret over something you did or didn't do can refuse to let go for a long time. It shows what matters to you. Heidegger described a remarkable feature of existence: in choosing one possibility, we inevitably leave others behind. He saw this not as a personal mistake but as the very structure of human life — no one can live out all their possibilities. Moreover, for Heidegger the past is neither closed nor dead: we go on carrying it, and its meaning changes depending on how we live on. From this point of view, your regret is not a verdict but a sign that the past is still taking part in your life. You decide what it will become as things continue.
regret.practice: Finish: “Back then I didn't choose…, but the fact that it mattered to me I can keep like this: …”

longing.text: Longing for a particular person is a deep feeling, and there's nothing shameful in it. Merleau-Ponty described the “phantom limb” in detail: after a loss, the body goes on feeling an arm or a leg and still reaches out to the world through it. He explained this by saying that the body preserves a habitual way of being in the world. From this point of view, you might say there's something similar in longing: for years your world was arranged with this person in it — their voice in the evenings, their place at the table, a shared rhythm. Your body and habits keep reaching for them. This isn't weakness but the memory of your whole life. Longing gradually changes its shape as the world slowly rearranges itself, and there's no need to hurry it.
longing.practice: Notice one place or moment of the day where this person's absence is felt most strongly. Spend some time there, gently.

world_pain.text: Pain for the world, from hard news, violence and injustice, speaks of your capacity for compassion. Heidegger believed human beings are always “being-with-others”: even distant people are part of our world, and their suffering concerns us. The late Heidegger reflected a great deal on the dangers of the age, and in his essay “The Question Concerning Technology” he quoted Hölderlin's lines saying that where danger is, the saving power grows too. From this point of view, you can avoid turning away from the pain without drowning in it either. Merleau-Ponty would remind us that what we lean on is always bodily and concrete: people close to us, the ground under our feet, small good deeds. The world's pain is easier to carry when you're holding on to something nearby.
world_pain.practice: Put the news aside and name five things you can see around you. Then decide on one good thing you can do close by.

quote.text: But where danger is, grows the saving power also.
quote.author: Friedrich Hölderlin
quote.source: the hymn “Patmos”; quoted by Heidegger in “The Question Concerning Technology” (1953)

rejection.text: Rejection wounds deeply, and that's natural. Merleau-Ponty showed that we experience others first of all with the body: their gaze, their tone, a withdrawn gesture get inside us before we have time to make sense of them. So a refusal can feel like a blow, a tightness in the chest, a wish to hide. Heidegger would add that “being-with-others” is part of our very structure: we are open to others, and therefore vulnerable. From this point of view, your pain is not weakness but the price of this openness. One refusal doesn't cancel the fact that you exist among many people. You can let your body feel the blow — and then slowly take back your space.
rejection.practice: Notice where in your body the rejection echoes. Place your palm there and take three slow breaths out.

abandonment.text: The fear of being abandoned is a deep feeling, and it deserves gentleness. Heidegger wrote that a human being is by their very nature “being-with”: we always live in a world shared with others. He even observed that loneliness is also a way of being with others: we're lonely precisely because others are missing. From this point of view, the fear of being left is not a weakness of character but a sharp sense of how much we are woven from connections. Merleau-Ponty spoke of “intercorporeality” — the bodily intertwining of people with one another. The fear shows how much the people close to you mean to you. And it also reminds you that connection doesn't rest on one person: you are woven into a whole web.
abandonment.practice: Name five people or places you are connected with — even loosely. Picture these threads for a minute.

unrequited.text: Unrequited love wounds painfully, and your pain is real. Heidegger distinguished two forms of care for another. One “leaps in”: it takes over for the other and seeks to manage them. The other “leaps ahead”: it helps the other be free in their own possibilities. From this point of view, you might say the most caring love recognises the other's freedom, including their freedom not to answer. This doesn't make the pain smaller, but it gives your love dignity: you loved a person rather than trying to possess them. Merleau-Ponty would remind us that love lives in the body, and it needs time to change its shape.
unrequited.practice: Write: “I let you be free. And I allow myself to grieve.” Read it slowly.

humiliation.text: Humiliation is one of the most painful experiences, and it isn't your fault that you went through it. Merleau-Ponty described the body as something that both sees and is seen. In humiliation this balance breaks: it's as if you've been turned into an object put on display under someone else's gaze, and stripped of the role of the one who looks. Heidegger would call this the power of the impersonal “das Man,” which seems to pass a verdict in the name of “everyone.” From this point of view, humiliation is not the truth about you but a situation in which you were deprived of the position of a subject. You can take it back gradually: begin once more to see, to act, to speak in the first person.
humiliation.practice: Look around and name out loud three things you see. You are once again the one who looks.

body_shame.text: Unhappiness with your body is a very common and painful feeling. Merleau-Ponty distinguished the body looked at as an object — something that can be measured and judged — from the “lived body” through which we live: through which we see, touch, move, embrace. Body shame is when we start living only the first, constantly looking at ourselves from the outside, as if in a mirror. From this point of view, you can little by little return to your body from the inside: not how it looks, but what it lets you feel and do. Merleau-Ponty wrote that we don't “have” a body; we are a body. It is not a project to be corrected but your way of being in the world.
body_shame.practice: Make one simple movement — stretch, walk a little — and pay attention only to how it feels from the inside, not to how it looks.

illness.text: Illness, when your body lets you down, changes the whole world, and that's hard. Merleau-Ponty wrote that consciousness is originally not an “I think” but an “I can”: we live the world through the body's possibilities — to reach, to walk somewhere, to lift. When the body is ill, the world changes: stairs become an obstacle, the street becomes far away. This isn't a whim but a real change in how the world is given. From this point of view, your distress is understandable: you're losing not only strength but also your familiar world. But Merleau-Ponty also showed that the body is capable of rebuilding its “I can,” of finding new ways of being in the world. You can gently look for these new possibilities — however small they may be.
illness.practice: Name one “I can” you have today — even the smallest. Stay with it for a while.

quote.text: The body is our general medium for having a world.
quote.author: Maurice Merleau-Ponty

pride.text: Pride in what you've done is a healthy and deserved feeling. Heidegger wrote of the “work” as something in which a whole world is disclosed: a thing that has been made connects the maker's hands, the material, and the people it is meant for. Merleau-Ponty showed that consciousness is originally an “I can,” and that every skill mastered becomes part of the body. From this point of view, pride is the moment when your “I can” has taken form and become visible: this has been done, and I did it. It isn't boasting or comparison with others, but joy in a world that has grown wider. Let yourself stay with this feeling. Perhaps you'll notice that you're holding yourself differently right now — straighter, freer.
pride.practice: Look at what you've made and notice how you're standing or sitting. Let yourself stay in that posture for a minute.

melancholy.text: Gentle sadness is a quiet feeling in which sorrow is mixed with tenderness. It doesn't need to be “fixed.” Heidegger regarded moods not as random emotions but as ways in which the world is disclosed. In his lectures The Fundamental Concepts of Metaphysics, he opened the discussion of philosophy with Novalis's words about homesickness. From this point of view, you might say melancholy is a mood in which the world is disclosed in its fragility and depth: we feel how everything passes, and precisely for that reason we see how precious it is. Melancholy doesn't weaken but deepens: in it you seem closer to something essential. Allow yourself to stay in it, without hurrying to chase it away.
melancholy.practice: Choose some music, or a window you can sit by for five minutes, and simply let this mood be.

quote.text: Philosophy is really homesickness, an urge to be at home everywhere.
quote.author: Novalis
quote.source: quoted by Heidegger in The Fundamental Concepts of Metaphysics (1929–1930)
